title: Employment Cost Index Q3 2026: Build Each Department's 2027 Hospital Labor Budget From Rate, Hours, and Mix Before You Apply 3.7% Across the Board
excerpt: The BLS Employment Cost Index released October 30, 2026 puts hospital compensation up 3.7% over the year and health benefits up 6.4%, while the FY 2027 Medicare inpatient update is 2.3%. Here is how a hospital finance team builds each department's 2027 hospital labor budget from rate, paid hours, and skill mix, with one med-surg unit worked through three futures the headline number matches in none.
author: FinBoard Team
coverAlt: Hospital finance analyst splitting a nursing unit's 2027 hospital labor budget into rate, paid hours, and skill mix beside the Q3 2026 Employment Cost Index release
content:
A hospital labor budget built by applying the 3.7% Employment Cost Index increase to last year's salary line will be wrong on every unit, in both directions. The ECI prices an hour of labor at fixed employment weights. A department's spend moves with rate, paid hours, and skill mix, and each needs its own line.

Why this matters now

On 2026-10-30 the Bureau of Labor Statistics released the Employment Cost Index for the third quarter of 2026. Compensation costs for civilian workers rose 0.8 percent for the quarter and 3.4 percent for the 12 months ended September. Benefit costs in private industry rose 3.9 percent over the year, wages and salaries rose 3.1 percent, and health benefits rose 6.4 percent. The industry table published the same day, 2026-10-30, puts hospitals at 1.0 percent for the quarter and 3.7 percent for the year, against 4.0 percent for health care and social assistance as a whole and 2.9 percent for nursing and residential care facilities.

Set that beside the payment side. The CMS FY 2027 IPPS final rule fact sheet, dated 2026-07-31, finalizes a 2.3 percent operating payment update for the fiscal year that began October 1, 2026: a 3.2 percent market basket less a 0.9 point productivity adjustment. Labor priced at 3.7 percent against inpatient rates updated at 2.3 percent is the arithmetic behind every 2027 budget meeting this month. For the dollar base, the BLS Employer Costs for Employee Compensation table for June 2026, released 2026-09-09, puts hospital compensation at $66.85 per hour worked, of which $43.88 is wages and $22.97 is benefits, with health insurance alone at $5.99.

Most coverage of the release reads it as an inflation signal for the Federal Reserve. That isn't the question a hospital finance team has in November. The question is what number goes on each department's 2027 salary, benefits, and contract labor lines, and the ECI answers only one third of it. This article separates the three parts, works one nursing unit through, and sets the controls so the budget survives review.

What the ECI measures and what a department budget needs

A self-contained definition first. The Employment Cost Index measures the change in the cost of an hour of labor at fixed employment weights. BLS holds the employment count in each occupation and industry cell constant, so the index moves when wage rates and benefit costs move, and it does not move when a hospital shifts hours from agency nurses to employed nurses, from RNs to nursing assistants, or from one unit to another. The BLS methods handbook describes the ECI as a modified Laspeyres index for exactly this reason.

A department's labor spend is a different object. It is rate times paid hours, summed over each class of worker, plus benefits that follow some of those hours and some of those heads. Three levers move it, and the ECI speaks to only the first.

Rate is dollars per paid hour for employed staff, moved by merit cycles, market adjustments, shift differentials, and the overtime share. The ECI is a reasonable external check on this lever and on nothing else.

Hours are paid hours, productive and nonproductive, driven by volume and the staffing standard. For a nursing unit the standard is paid hours per patient day. For a laboratory or imaging department it is hours per billable test or exam. Volume comes from the operating plan, not from BLS.

Mix is who supplies the hours: employed RN, LPN, nursing assistant, per diem, agency. An agency hour bills at roughly twice an employed wage and carries no benefit load on the hospital's books. A unit that converts 3,000 agency hours to employed hours cuts its spend while its average employed rate rises. A unit that can't hire does the opposite.

One nursing unit, worked from the September books

Four West is a 32-bed medical-surgical unit. The figures are illustrative. The method is the point. The finance analyst pulls the January through September 2026 general ledger and payroll register and annualizes both.

Step one: the 2026 base, in hours and dollars

Annualized 2026 salaries and wages are $5,460,000 over 124,000 paid hours, an average of $44.03 per paid hour, close to the BLS hospital wage figure. Benefits are $1,870,000, of which $660,000 is health insurance and $1,210,000 is FICA, retirement match, and paid time off accrual. Contract labor is $410,000 for 4,100 agency hours at $100 an hour, booked to purchased services. Total labor is $7,740,000. Patient days are 10,400, so the unit ran 12.32 paid hours per patient day including agency.

Step two: the across-the-board number

Multiply $7,740,000 by 1.037 and the 2027 line is $8,026,000. It takes one minute. It is defensible in no meeting, because nobody can say which part of it is a raise, which part is volume, and which part is agency.

Step three: rate

The merit cycle is 3.0 percent effective April 1, which is 2.25 percent on a calendar-year basis. A market adjustment for RNs of 2.0 percent takes effect January 1, and RN wages are 60 percent of the unit's wage base, so it adds 1.2 percent. The employed rate for 2027 is $44.03 times 1.0345, or $45.55. That is a 3.45 percent rate increase, in the neighborhood of the 3.7 percent ECI figure, and it is the only place the ECI belongs in this budget.

Step four: hours

The 2027 operating plan calls for 10,700 patient days, up 2.9 percent. The nursing director's staffing standard is 11.9 paid hours per patient day, below the 12.32 the unit actually ran, because the plan fills two open RN positions and stops using agency to cover them. Total paid hours are 11.9 times 10,700, or 127,330. Volume went up and hours went down. No percentage applied to last year's dollars produces that result.

Step five: mix and benefits

The plan keeps 1,200 agency hours for seasonal peaks at $98 an hour, or $117,600, and puts the other 126,130 hours on the employed rate: 126,130 times $45.55 is $5,745,000. Benefits split in two. FICA, retirement, and PTO accrual follow wages at the 2026 ratio of 22.16 percent, which gives $1,273,000. Health insurance follows heads, not hours. The 2026 cost per FTE was $660,000 over 59.6 FTEs, or $11,074, and a 6.4 percent increase in line with the ECI health benefit figure takes it to $11,783. At 60.6 FTEs for 2027 that is $714,000. Benefits total $1,987,000.

Step six: compare three futures

Built from the levers, Four West's 2027 labor budget is $5,745,000 plus $1,987,000 plus $117,600, about $7,850,000. The across-the-board figure was $8,026,000, which overstates this unit by about $176,000. Now hold productivity at 11.9 but assume the two RN positions stay open and agency hours stay at 4,100, at $103 an hour. Employed hours fall to 123,230 and the line lands near $7,977,000. Finally assume nothing changes except volume: 12.32 hours per patient day and 4,100 agency hours. The line is about $8,253,000, which is $227,000 above the headline number.

Three defensible futures, and the 3.7 percent figure matched none of them. More to the point, when the actual comes in at $8,100,000 next October, the built budget tells the director whether rate, hours, or agency moved. The headline budget tells nobody anything.

Accounting controls for the hospital labor budget

Source data: the general ledger salary, benefit, and purchased services accounts by department for January through September 2026 with the annualization method written down; the payroll register by pay period with paid hours split productive and nonproductive and by job code; agency invoices with hours and bill rates; the time and attendance export; the volume statistics the operating plan uses, patient days for nursing and billable units elsewhere; the approved merit and market adjustment schedule with effective dates; the health plan renewal letter; the BLS ECI release and industry table; and the FY 2027 IPPS fact sheet for the payment side.

Calculation: a fixed sequence anyone on the team can re-perform. Base rate equals annualized wages divided by paid hours. The 2027 rate equals base rate times one plus each adjustment, weighted by its months in effect and its share of the wage base. Hours equal the staffing standard times planned volume. Employed wages equal employed hours times rate. Statutory and retirement benefits equal wages times the prior-year ratio. Health insurance equals cost per FTE times the renewal increase times planned FTEs. Agency equals agency hours times the contracted bill rate. Labor expense is a flow measured over the fiscal period. Accrued payroll and the PTO liability are point-in-time balances the budget does not restate. Polarity matters on one account in particular: salaries, benefits, and agency are all debits to expense, but agency sits in purchased services, not in salaries, so a budget that nets agency savings against salary variance has mixed two accounts and will not reconcile to the ledger.

Review: a second analyst rebuilds one unit from the same payroll register and lands within rounding; the sum of department paid hours agrees to the payroll register total for the base period; rate increases agree to the approved compensation schedule and its effective dates; the staffing standard on each unit is signed by the department director; agency hours in the plan agree to the agency reduction plan the chief nursing officer approved; and any department whose built budget differs from the across-the-board figure by more than 3 percent in either direction carries a one-line explanation naming the lever.

Decision: the department director owns the hours and mix assumptions. Human resources and the compensation committee own the rate. The CFO owns the total and the decision to fund positions instead of agency. Finance owns the worksheet, its date, and the monthly variance split into rate, hours, and mix, which is the report the payment-side reviews and the payer mix review get compared against when margin moves.

Limits and common mistakes

The ECI industry figures are national. A hospital in a market where RN wages moved 6 percent should budget the local number and note the national one. The civilian and private industry tables both show 3.7 percent for hospitals this quarter, but the quarterly figures are not seasonally adjusted at the industry level, so compare 12-month changes, not quarters. Every dollar figure for Four West is illustrative, and the health insurance increase in the example uses the ECI benefit figure as a placeholder for a renewal letter that should replace it.

The first mistake is applying the ECI percentage to total labor including agency. Agency is a purchased service with its own rate and its own hours, and the index excludes mix shifts by construction.

The second is budgeting health insurance per hour. Premiums follow enrolled heads. A unit that adds overtime adds no premium, and a unit that fills two vacancies adds two.

The third is annualizing merit as if it took effect January 1. A 3 percent raise effective April 1 is 2.25 percent on the calendar year, and the gap shows up as a favorable first-quarter variance that nobody can explain.

The fourth is counting an agency reduction twice, once as fewer agency hours and again as a lower average rate, when the employed rate actually rises as agency leaves the base.

The fifth is budgeting productive hours only. Paid time off, orientation, and education are paid hours that produce no patient care, and a standard that leaves them out will be under-budgeted from the first pay period. Employer payroll taxes have their own month-by-month shape as well, and the wage base phasing method applies to a hospital's FICA line the same way it applies to any employer.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should a hospital labor budget use the Employment Cost Index as its increase?

Only for the rate lever. The Employment Cost Index measures the change in the cost of an hour of labor at fixed employment weights, so it says nothing about a department's paid hours, volume, or agency mix. Use it as an external check on the merit and market rate assumption, then build hours from the staffing standard and planned volume and build mix from the hiring plan.

What did the Q3 2026 Employment Cost Index say about hospitals?

The release dated October 30, 2026 shows hospital compensation costs up 1.0 percent for the three months and 3.7 percent for the 12 months ended September 2026, compared with 3.4 percent for all civilian workers and 4.0 percent for health care and social assistance. Private industry health benefit costs rose 6.4 percent over the same 12 months.

How should agency or contract labor be handled in a department labor budget?

As its own line in purchased services, budgeted as agency hours times the contracted bill rate, never as part of salaries. Converting agency hours to employed hours lowers total spend while raising the average employed rate, so the budget must show the hours moving between the two lines rather than netting them.

Why is health insurance budgeted per FTE instead of per hour?

Because the premium follows enrolled heads, not hours worked. A unit that adds overtime hours does not add premium cost, and a unit that fills two vacancies does. Budget health insurance as cost per FTE times the renewal increase times planned FTEs, and keep FICA, retirement match, and PTO accrual on the wage-driven ratio.

How does the 2.3 percent FY 2027 IPPS update relate to the labor budget?

It is the Medicare inpatient operating rate update that took effect October 1, 2026, built from a 3.2 percent market basket less a 0.9 point productivity adjustment. Labor priced at 3.7 percent against rates updated at 2.3 percent is the margin gap the built budget has to explain, lever by lever, before the board sees it.

Once each department's budget is written as rate, hours, and mix, the monthly variance stops being a single unexplained number. FinBoard reads the general ledger by class and department into one budget versus actual view, so the dollar side of every unit's salary, benefit, and purchased services variance is on one page each month, and the hours side from the payroll register has a figure to reconcile to.
